concepts.title: Criticism
concepts.hook: A teammate misses a deadline. A sharp remark may feel quick, yet it may not help with the next deadline. What could you ask first?
concepts.rule: Carnegie urges us to avoid blame and look for the other person's reasons. When a real error needs fixing, name the task with care; that added step is informed by feedback research.

claims.text: Carnegie's advice in Part One, chapter 1: avoid blame and try to understand why people act as they do.
What research says: Feedback helped work on average. Yet more than one third of the 607 effects were bad. This does not mean we should avoid all checks.
What research says: The review says feedback may work best when it points to the task. A focus on the self may hurt. The results vary.

concepts.title: Appreciation
concepts.hook: A colleague stays late to help with a report. A plain thank you may matter more than a broad compliment. What would you name?
concepts.rule: Notice a real act and thank the person for it. Keep the words true and specific. Praise is not a sure way to get more work from someone.

claims.text: Part One, chapter 2: Carnegie says to give true thanks for a real act. Flattery does not count.
What research says: In four tests, thanks led to more help or effort. Those thanked felt more valued. This may not hold for all people.

What research says: A review of research on children argues that praise may help, hurt, or have little effect on interest in a task, depending on its form and setting. It does not establish the same pattern for adults.

concepts.title: Shared interest
concepts.hook: You want help with a weekend task. The other person has plans too. What changes when you ask what matters to them before making a plan?
concepts.rule: First learn what the other person wants. If your proposal truly serves that aim, explain the benefit from their point of view and leave them free to choose.

claims.text: Part One, chapter 3: Carnegie says to find out what the other person wants. Show how your plan may help, if it can.
What research says: A review of 72 work studies found a link. Staff who felt they had a choice had more drive from within. This does not test one request.
What research says: A review of ten work trials found seven with mostly good results, two mixed, and one with no clear change. Staff changed less than leaders. Each study had some risk of bias.
